title: Rayleigh scattering - Wikipedia

blocks.text: Rayleigh scattering causes the blue color of the sky at large angles to the direction of solar rays and yellow or orange colors for light from the direction of the Sun.[1]

Rayleigh scattering (/ˈreɪli/ RAY-lee) is the scattering or deflection of light, or other electromagnetic radiation, by particles with a size much smaller than the wavelength of the radiation. For light frequencies well below the resonance frequency of the scattering medium (normal dispersion regime), the amount of scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength (e.g., a blue color is scattered much more than a red color as light propagates through air). The phenomenon is named after the 19th-century British physicist Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt).[2]

Due to Rayleigh scattering, red and orange colors are more visible during sunset because the blue and violet light has been scattered out of the direct path. This can yield dramatically colored skies and monochromatic rainbows.
dramatically colored skies
monochromatic rainbows

Rayleigh scattering results from the electric polarizability of the particles. The oscillating electric field of a light wave acts on the charges within a particle, causing them to move at the same frequency. The particle, therefore, becomes a small radiating dipole whose radiation we see as scattered light. The particles may be individual atoms or molecules; it can occur when light travels through transparent solids and liquids, but is most prominently seen in gases.

Rayleigh scattering of sunlight in Earth's atmosphere causes diffuse sky radiation. Since blue light wavelengths scatter more, the diffuse sky seen in daytime is blue. At twilight the sunlight on the horizon is missing the scattered blue light wavelengths giving a yellowish to reddish hue to the low Sun.[1]

Scattering by particles with a size comparable to, or larger than, the wavelength of the light is typically treated by the Mie theory, the discrete dipole approximation and other computational techniques. Rayleigh scattering applies to particles that are small with respect to wavelengths of light, and that are optically "soft" (i.e., with a refractive index close to 1). Anomalous diffraction theory applies to optically soft but larger particles.
History

In c. 1506–1510, Leonardo da Vinci conjectured that the scattering of sunlight by small particles in the atmosphere gave the sky its blue hue, and analysis of his paintings suggest that he understood the influence of particle size on the scattering of light.[3]

In 1869, while attempting to determine whether any contaminants remained in the purified air he used for infrared experiments, John Tyndall discovered that bright light scattering off nanoscopic particulates was faintly blue-tinted.[4] While he proposed that this phenomenon explained the blueness of the sky, he could not explain the preference for blue light, nor could atmospheric dust explain the intensity of the sky's color.[1]

In 1871, Lord Rayleigh published two papers on the color and polarization of skylight to quantify Tyndall's effect in water droplets in terms of the tiny particulates' volumes and refractive indices.[5][6][7] In 1881, with the benefit of James Clerk Maxwell's 1865 proof of the electromagnetic nature of light, he showed that his equations followed from electromagnetism.[8] In 1899, he showed that they applied to individual molecules, with terms containing particulate volumes and refractive indices replaced with terms for molecular polarizability.[9] It was this paper that established the basic scientific model for the color of the sky.[1]

The size of a scattering particle is often parameterized by the ratio

At the intermediate x ≃ 1 of Mie scattering, interference effects develop through phase variations over the object's surface. Rayleigh scattering applies to the case when the scattering particle is very small (x ≪ 1, with a particle size < 1/10 of wavelength[10]) and the whole surface re-radiates with the same phase. The major constituent of the atmosphere, nitrogen, has Rayleigh cross section of 5.1×10−31 m2 at a wavelength of 532 nm (green light).[15] Over the length of one meter the fraction of light scattered can be approximated from the product of the cross-section and the particle density, that is number of particles per unit volume. For air at atmospheric pressure there are about 2×1025 molecules per cubic meter, and the fraction scattered will be 10−5 for every meter of travel.[citation needed]

Cause of the blue color of the sky

The blue color of the sky is a consequence of three factors:[18]
the blackbody spectrum of sunlight coming into the Earth's atmosphere,
Rayleigh scattering of that light off oxygen and nitrogen molecules, and
the response of the human visual system.

The strong wavelength dependence of the Rayleigh scattering (~λ−4) means that shorter (blue) wavelengths are scattered more strongly than longer (red) wavelengths. This results in the indirect blue and violet light coming from all regions of the sky. The human eye responds to this wavelength combination as if it were a combination of blue and white light.[18]

Some of the scattering can also be from sulfate particles. For years after large Plinian eruptions, the blue cast of the sky is notably brightened by the persistent sulfate load of the stratospheric gases. Some works of the artist J. M. W. Turner may owe their vivid red colours to the eruption of Mount Tambora in his lifetime.[19]

In locations with little light pollution, the moonlit night sky is also blue, because moonlight is reflected sunlight, with a slightly lower color temperature due to the brownish color of the Moon. The moonlit sky is not perceived as blue, however, because at low light levels human vision comes mainly from rod cells that do not produce any color perception (Purkinje effect).[20]
Of sound in amorphous solids

Rayleigh scattering is also an important mechanism of wave scattering in amorphous solids such as glass, and is responsible for acoustic wave damping and phonon damping in glasses and granular matter at low or not too high temperatures.[21] This is because in glasses at higher temperatures the Rayleigh-type scattering regime is obscured by the anharmonic damping (typically with a ~λ−2 dependence on wavelength), which becomes increasingly more important as the temperature rises.
In amorphous solids – glasses – optical fibers

Rayleigh scattering is an important component of the scattering of optical signals in optical fibers. Silica fibers are glasses, disordered materials with microscopic variations of density and refractive index. These give rise to energy losses due to the scattered light, with the following coefficient:[22] α scat = 8 π 3 3 λ 4 n 8 p 2 k T f β {\displaystyle \alpha _{\text{scat}}={\frac {8\pi ^{3}}{3\lambda ^{4}}}n^{8}p^{2}kT_{\text{f}}\beta }

where n is the refraction index, p is the photoelastic coefficient of the glass, k is the Boltzmann constant, and β is the isothermal compressibility. Tf is a fictive temperature, representing the temperature at which the density fluctuations are "frozen" in the material.
In porous materials
opalescent

Rayleigh-type λ−4 scattering can also be exhibited by porous materials. An example is the strong optical scattering by nanoporous materials.[24] The strong contrast in refractive index between pores and solid parts of sintered alumina results in very strong scattering, with light completely changing direction each five micrometers on average. The λ−4-type scattering is caused by the nanoporous structure (a narrow pore size distribution around ~70 nm) obtained by sintering monodispersive alumina powder.

For the wireless communication effect, see <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_fading" title="Rayleigh fading">Rayleigh fading</a>.</div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arctic_Sunset.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arctic_Sunset.jpg" src="data:image/jpeg;base64," decoding="async" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1701" data-file-type="bitmap" height="197" width="300" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBw" data-pg-id="n0"></a><figcaption id="mwCA">Rayleigh scattering causes the blue color of the sky at large angles to the direction of solar rays and yellow or orange colors for light from the direction of the Sun.<sup about="#mwt6" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bohren-2007_1-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bohren-2007"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Bohren-2007-1"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bohren-2007-1" id="mwCQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCw">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwDA">]</span></span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwDQ" data-pg-id="n1"><b id="mwDg">Rayleigh scattering</b> (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap" about="#mwt7" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwDw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"IPAc-en","href":"./Template:IPAc-en"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"ˈ"},"2":{"wt":"r"},"3":{"wt":"eɪ"},"4":{"wt":"l"},"5":{"wt":"i"}},"i":0}}]}"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="'r' in 'rye'">r</span><span title="/eɪ/: 'a' in 'face'">eɪ</span><span title="'l' in 'lie'">l</span><span title="/i/: 'y' in 'happy'">i</span></span>/</a></span></span> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key" title="Help:Pronunciation respelling key" about="#mwt8" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwEA" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"respell","href":"./Template:Respell"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"RAY"},"2":{"wt":"lee"}},"i":0}}]}"><i title="English pronunciation respelling"><span style="font-size:90%">RAY</span>-lee</i></a>) is the scattering or deflection of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light" title="Light" id="mwEQ">light</a>, or other <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation" title="Electromagnetic radiation" id="mwEg">electromagnetic radiation</a>, by particles with a size much smaller than the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength" title="Wavelength" id="mwEw">wavelength</a> of the radiation. For light frequencies well below the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonance" title="Resonance" id="mwFA">resonance</a> frequency of the scattering medium (normal <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dispersion_relation" title="Dispersion relation" id="mwFQ">dispersion</a> regime), the amount of scattering is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversely_proportional" title="Inversely proportional" class="mw-redirect" id="mwFg">inversely proportional</a> to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_power" title="Fourth power" id="mwFw">fourth power</a> of the wavelength (e.g., a blue color is scattered much more than a red color as light propagates through air). The phenomenon is named after the 19th-century British physicist <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Rayleigh" title="Lord Rayleigh" class="mw-redirect" id="mwGA">Lord Rayleigh</a> (John William Strutt).<sup about="#mwt9" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-2"}}"><a href="#cite_note-2" id="mwGQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwGg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwGw">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwHA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwHQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monochrome_Rainbow.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwHg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monochrome_Rainbow.jpg" src="data:image/jpeg;base64," decoding="async" data-file-width="4032" data-file-height="2419" data-file-type="bitmap" height="180" width="300" class="mw-file-element" id="mwHw" data-pg-id="n2"></a><figcaption id="mwIA">Due to Rayleigh scattering, red and orange colors are more visible during sunset because the blue and violet light has been scattered out of the direct path. This can yield <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_optics#Sky_coloration" title="Atmospheric optics" id="mwIQ" data-pg-id="n3">dramatically colored skies</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monochrome_rainbow" title="Monochrome rainbow" id="mwIg" data-pg-id="n4">monochromatic rainbows</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwIw" data-pg-id="n5">Rayleigh scattering results from the electric <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarizability" title="Polarizability" id="mwJA">polarizability</a> of the particles. The oscillating electric field of a light wave acts on the charges within a particle, causing them to move at the same frequency. The particle, therefore, becomes a small radiating <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dipole" title="Dipole" id="mwJQ">dipole</a> whose radiation we see as scattered light. The particles may be individual atoms or molecules; it can occur when light travels through transparent solids and liquids, but is most prominently seen in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas" title="Gas" id="mwJg">gases</a>.</p>

<p id="mwJw" data-pg-id="n6">Rayleigh scattering of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mwKA">sunlight</a> in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere" title="Earth's atmosphere" class="mw-redirect" id="mwKQ">Earth's atmosphere</a> causes <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuse_sky_radiation" title="Diffuse sky radiation" id="mwKg">diffuse sky radiation</a>. Since blue light wavelengths scatter more, the diffuse sky seen in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime" title="Daytime" id="mwKw">daytime</a> is blue. At <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight" title="Twilight" id="mwLA">twilight</a> the sunlight on the horizon is missing the scattered blue light wavelengths giving a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_hour_(photography)" title="Golden hour (photography)" id="mwLQ">yellowish</a> to reddish hue to the low <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun" title="Sun" id="mwLg">Sun</a>.<sup about="#mwt10" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bohren-2007_1-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bohren-2007"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bohren-2007-1" id="mwLw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwMA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwMQ">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwMg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwMw" data-pg-id="n7">Scattering by particles with a size comparable to, or larger than, the wavelength of the light is typically treated by the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_theory" title="Mie theory" class="mw-redirect" id="mwNA">Mie theory</a>, the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_dipole_approximation" title="Discrete dipole approximation" id="mwNQ">discrete dipole approximation</a> and other computational techniques. Rayleigh scattering applies to particles that are small with respect to wavelengths of light, and that are optically "soft" (i.e., with a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractive_index" title="Refractive index" id="mwNg">refractive index</a> close to 1). <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalous_diffraction_theory" title="Anomalous diffraction theory" id="mwNw">Anomalous diffraction theory</a> applies to optically soft but larger particles.</p>

<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" id="mwOA" data-mw="{"autoGenerated":true}"></section><section data-mw-section-id="1" id="mwOQ" aria-labelledby="History"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History" data-pg-id="n8">History</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Rayleigh_scattering&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwOg" data-pg-id="n9">In c. 1506–1510, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci" title="Leonardo da Vinci" id="mwOw">Leonardo da Vinci</a> conjectured that the scattering of sunlight by small particles in the atmosphere gave the sky its <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuse_sky_radiation" title="Diffuse sky radiation" id="mwPA">blue hue</a>, and analysis of his paintings suggest that he understood the influence of particle size on the scattering of light.<sup about="#mwt13" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-3"}}"><a href="#cite_note-3" id="mwPQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwPg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwPw">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwQA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwQQ" data-pg-id="n10">In 1869, while attempting to determine whether any contaminants remained in the purified air he used for infrared experiments, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tyndall" title="John Tyndall" id="mwQg">John Tyndall</a> discovered that bright light scattering off nanoscopic particulates was faintly blue-tinted.<sup about="#mwt16" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-4" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-4"}}"><a href="#cite_note-4" id="mwQw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwRA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwRQ">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwRg">]</span></span></a></sup> While he proposed that this phenomenon explained the blueness of the sky, he could not explain the preference for blue light, nor could atmospheric dust explain the intensity of the sky's color.<sup about="#mwt17" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bohren-2007_1-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bohren-2007"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bohren-2007-1" id="mwRw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwSA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwSQ">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwSg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwSw" data-pg-id="n11">In 1871, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Rayleigh" title="Lord Rayleigh" class="mw-redirect" id="mwTA">Lord Rayleigh</a> published two papers on the color and polarization of skylight to quantify <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyndall_effect" title="Tyndall effect" id="mwTQ">Tyndall's effect</a> in water droplets in terms of the tiny particulates' volumes and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractive_index" title="Refractive index" id="mwTg">refractive indices</a>.<sup about="#mwt20" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-5" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-5"}}"><a href="#cite_note-5" id="mwTw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwUA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwUQ">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwUg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt23" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-6" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-6"}}"><a href="#cite_note-6" id="mwUw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwVA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwVQ">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwVg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt26" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-7" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-7"}}"><a href="#cite_note-7" id="mwVw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwWA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWQ">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWg">]</span></span></a></sup> In 1881, with the benefit of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell" title="James Clerk Maxwell" id="mwWw">James Clerk Maxwell</a>'s 1865 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Maxwell's_equations" title="History of Maxwell's equations" id="mwXA">proof of the electromagnetic nature of light</a>, he showed that his equations followed from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetism" title="Electromagnetism" id="mwXQ">electromagnetism</a>.<sup about="#mwt29" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-8" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-8"}}"><a href="#cite_note-8" id="mwXg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwXw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwYA">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwYQ">]</span></span></a></sup> In 1899, he showed that they applied to individual molecules, with terms containing particulate volumes and refractive indices replaced with terms for molecular <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarizability" title="Polarizability" id="mwYg">polarizability</a>.<sup about="#mwt32" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-9" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-9"}}"><a href="#cite_note-9" id="mwYw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwZA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwZQ">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwZg">]</span></span></a></sup>
It was this paper that established the basic scientific model for the color of the sky.<sup about="#mwt33" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bohren-2007_1-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bohren-2007"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bohren-2007-1" id="mwZw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwaA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwaQ">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwag">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="2" id="mwaw" aria-labelledby="Small_size_parameter_approximation"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Small_size_parameter_approximation" data-pg-id="n12">Small size parameter approximation</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Rayleigh_scattering&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Small size parameter approximation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>

At the intermediate x ≃ 1 of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_scattering" title="Mie scattering" id="mwdQ">Mie scattering</a>, interference effects develop through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_(waves)" title="Phase (waves)" id="mwdg">phase</a> variations over the object's surface. Rayleigh scattering applies to the case when the scattering particle is very small (x ≪ 1, with a particle size < 1/10 of wavelength<sup about="#mwt35" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-10" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-10"}}"><a href="#cite_note-10" id="mwdw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mweA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mweQ">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket" id="mweg">]</span></span></a></sup>) and the whole surface re-radiates with the same phase. Because the particles are randomly positioned, the scattered light arrives at a particular point with a random collection of phases; it is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" </section><section data-mw-section-id="5" id="mwzQ" aria-labelledby="Cause_of_the_blue_color_of_the_sky"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Cause_of_the_blue_color_of_the_sky" data-pg-id="n32">Cause of the blue color of the sky</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Rayleigh_scattering&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Cause of the blue color of the sky"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt70" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwzg" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Diffuse sky radiation"}},"i":0}}]}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt70" id="mwzw">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuse_sky_radiation" title="Diffuse sky radiation">Diffuse sky radiation</a></div>

<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mw0A"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CircularPolarizer.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mw0Q"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CircularPolarizer.jpg" src="data:image/jpeg;base64," decoding="async" data-file-width="2484" data-file-height="946" data-file-type="bitmap" height="95" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mw0g"></a><figcaption id="mw0w">Scattered blue light is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarization_(waves)" title="Polarization (waves)" id="mw1A" data-pg-id="n33">polarized</a>. The picture on the right is shot through a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarizing_filter_(photography)" title="Polarizing filter (photography)" id="mw1Q" data-pg-id="n34">polarizing filter</a>: the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarizer" title="Polarizer" id="mw1g" data-pg-id="n35">polarizer</a> transmits light that is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_polarization" title="Linear polarization" id="mw1w" data-pg-id="n36">linearly polarized</a> in a specific direction.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mw2A" data-pg-id="n37">The blue color of the sky is a consequence of three factors:<sup about="#mwt74" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-SmithAJP2005_18-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"SmithAJP2005"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-SmithAJP2005-18"}}"><a href="#cite_note-SmithAJP2005-18" id="mw2Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw2g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw2w">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw3A">]</span></span></a></sup></p> 
<ul id="mw3Q"><li id="mw3g" data-pg-id="n38">the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackbody_radiation" title="Blackbody radiation" class="mw-redirect" id="mw3w">blackbody</a> spectrum of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mw4A">sunlight</a> coming into the Earth's atmosphere,</li>
<li id="mw4Q" data-pg-id="n39">Rayleigh scattering of that light off oxygen and nitrogen molecules, and</li>
<li id="mw4g" data-pg-id="n40">the response of the human visual system.</li></ul>

<p id="mw4w" data-pg-id="n41">The strong wavelength dependence of the Rayleigh scattering (~<i id="mw5A">λ</i><sup id="mw5Q">−4</sup>) means that shorter (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue" title="Blue" id="mw5g">blue</a>) wavelengths are scattered more strongly than longer (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red" title="Red" id="mw5w">red</a>) wavelengths. This results in the indirect blue and violet light coming from all regions of the sky. The human eye responds to this wavelength combination as if it were a combination of blue and white light.<sup about="#mwt75" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-SmithAJP2005_18-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"SmithAJP2005"}}"><a href="#cite_note-SmithAJP2005-18" id="mw6A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw6Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw6g">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw6w">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mw7A" data-pg-id="n42">Some of the scattering can also be from sulfate particles. For years after large <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plinian_eruption" title="Plinian eruption" id="mw7Q">Plinian eruptions</a>, the blue cast of the sky is notably brightened by the persistent sulfate load of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratospheric" title="Stratospheric" class="mw-redirect" id="mw7g">stratospheric</a> gases. Some works of the artist <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._M._W._Turner" title="J. M. W. Turner" id="mw7w">J. M. W. Turner</a> may owe their vivid red colours to the eruption of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Tambora" title="Mount Tambora" id="mw8A">Mount Tambora</a> in his lifetime.<sup about="#mwt78" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-zerefos_19-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"zerefos"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-zerefos-19"}}"><a href="#cite_note-zerefos-19" id="mw8Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw8g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw8w">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw9A">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mw9Q" data-pg-id="n43">In locations with little <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_pollution" title="Light pollution" id="mw9g">light pollution</a>, the moonlit night sky is also blue, because moonlight is reflected sunlight, with a slightly lower <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_temperature" title="Color temperature" id="mw9w">color temperature</a> due to the brownish color of the Moon. The moonlit sky is not perceived as blue, however, because at low light levels human vision comes mainly from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_cells" title="Rod cells" class="mw-redirect" id="mw-A">rod cells</a> that do not produce any color perception (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purkinje_effect" title="Purkinje effect" id="mw-Q">Purkinje effect</a>).<sup about="#mwt81" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-20" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-20"}}"><a href="#cite_note-20" id="mw-g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw-w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw_A">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw_Q">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="6" id="mw_g" aria-labelledby="Of_sound_in_amorphous_solids"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Of_sound_in_amorphous_solids" data-pg-id="n44">Of sound in amorphous solids</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Rayleigh_scattering&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Of sound in amorphous solids"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mw_w" data-pg-id="n45">Rayleigh scattering is also an important mechanism of wave scattering in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_solids" title="Amorphous solids" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAQA">amorphous solids</a> such as glass, and is responsible for acoustic wave damping and phonon damping in glasses and granular matter at low or not too high temperatures.<sup about="#mwt84" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-21" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-21"}}"><a href="#cite_note-21" id="mwAQE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQM">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQQ">]</span></span></a></sup> This is because in glasses at higher temperatures the Rayleigh-type scattering regime is obscured by the anharmonic damping (typically with a ~<i id="mwAQU">λ</i><sup id="mwAQY">−2</sup> dependence on wavelength), which becomes increasingly more important as the temperature rises.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="7" id="mwAQc" aria-labelledby="In_amorphous_solids_–_glasses_–_optical_fibers"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="In_amorphous_solids_–_glasses_–_optical_fibers" data-pg-id="n46"><span id="In_amorphous_solids_.E2.80.93_glasses_.E2.80.93_optical_fibers" typeof="mw:FallbackId"></span>In amorphous solids – glasses – optical fibers</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Rayleigh_scattering&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: In amorphous solids – glasses – optical fibers"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwAQg" data-pg-id="n47">Rayleigh scattering is an important component of the scattering of optical signals in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_fibers" title="Optical fibers" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAQk">optical fibers</a>. Silica fibers are glasses,  disordered materials with microscopic variations of density and refractive index. These give rise to energy losses due to the scattered light, with the following coefficient:<sup about="#mwt87" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-22" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-22"}}"><a href="#cite_note-22" id="mwAQo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQw">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQ0">]</span></span></a></sup>
<span class="mwe-math-element mwe-math-element-block" typeof="mw:Extension/math" about="#mwt88" id="mwAQ4" data-mw="{"name":"math","attrs":{"display":"block"},"body":{"extsrc":"\\alpha_\\text{scat} = \\frac{8 \\pi^3}{3 \\lambda^4} n^8 p^2 k T_\\text{f} \\beta"}}"><span class="mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="mathjax_ignore" display="block" alttext="{\displaystyle \alpha _{\text{scat}}={\frac {8\pi ^{3}}{3\lambda ^{4}}}n^{8}p^{2}kT_{\text{f}}\beta }">

</section><section data-mw-section-id="8" id="mwARg" aria-labelledby="In_porous_materials"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="In_porous_materials" data-pg-id="n49">In porous materials</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Rayleigh_scattering&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: In porous materials"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwARk"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Why_is_the_sky_blue.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwARo"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Why_is_the_sky_blue.jpg" src="data:image/jpeg;base64," decoding="async" data-file-width="1280" data-file-height="943" data-file-type="bitmap" height="184" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwARs"></a><figcaption id="mwARw">Rayleigh scattering in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opalescence" title="Opalescence" id="mwAR0" data-pg-id="n50">opalescent</a> glass: it appears blue from the side, but orange light shines through.<sup about="#mwt89" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-23" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-23"}}"><a href="#cite_note-23" id="mwAR4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAR8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASA">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASE">]</span></span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwASI" data-pg-id="n51">Rayleigh-type <i id="mwASM">λ</i><sup id="mwASQ">−4</sup> scattering can also be exhibited by porous materials. An example is the strong optical scattering by nanoporous materials.<sup about="#mwt92" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Svensson_24-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Svensson"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Svensson-24"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Svensson-24" id="mwASU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwASY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASc">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASg">]</span></span></a></sup> The strong contrast in refractive index between pores and solid parts of sintered <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alumina" title="Alumina" class="mw-redirect" id="mwASk">alumina</a> results in very strong scattering, with light completely changing direction each five micrometers on average. The <i id="mwASo">λ</i><sup id="mwASs">−4</sup>-type scattering is caused by the nanoporous structure (a narrow pore size distribution around ~70<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwASw"> </span>nm) obtained by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintering" title="Sintering" id="mwAS0">sintering</a> monodispersive alumina powder.</p>
